title: TempleOS system design (single-address-space, ring-0)
summary: TempleOS is a 64-bit x86-64 OS with no kernel/user separation (all code runs in ring 0), single address space (no virtual memory, no MMU protection), cooperative multitasking (no preemption), and a JIT-compiled language (HolyC) that serves as both programming language and shell. Designed by Terry A. Davis (1993-2017).

ext.summary: TempleOS is a 64-bit x86-64 OS with no kernel/user separation (all code runs in ring 0), single address space (no virtual memory, no MMU protection), cooperative multitasking (no preemption), and a JIT-compiled language (HolyC) that serves as both programming language and shell. Designed by Terry A. Davis (1993-2017).

structure.meaning: No virtual memory. No MMU protection. All tasks share one address space. Pointers are physical addresses.
No kernel/user separation. All code runs in ring 0. No system calls (direct function calls).
No preemption. Tasks must voluntarily yield (Yield()). Simpler than preemptive but one runaway task freezes the system.
JIT-compiled C-like language. No main() function. Top-level expressions execute during compilation (REPL-like). No linker — single compilation unit.
VGA mode 13h (or similar). 16-color palette. Designed per 'God's instructions' (per Davis).
PC speaker (single voice). No sound card support.
No network drivers. Davis: 'networking would be reinventing the wheel.' Isolated by design.
RedSea is native (flat namespace, no directories, compression). FAT32 and ISO 9660 for compatibility.
HolyC compiles to native x86-64 code on the fly. No separate compilation step. No linker.
Entire OS written by one person (Terry A. Davis) over ~15 years.

notes: TempleOS demonstrates that a complete OS can be built by one person.
Radical simplification: no virtual memory, no protection rings, no linker, no networking.
Single address space + ring-0 = no system calls, no context switches, no page faults.
Cooperative multitasking is simpler but vulnerable to runaway tasks.
HolyC's JIT + no-main() + top-level execution = interactive programming environment.
No kernel/user separation means no security boundaries — acceptable for a personal/recreational OS.
TempleOS is often cited as an example of 'outsider art' in software.
Davis claimed the 640x480/16-color/single-voice specs were divinely inspired.
